description: A team of people who dreamed of space and are up to interesting challenge.
summary:
Sun, Earth and terrain for any point on Moon at any given moment. 
Using this web app, you can pick  pick a moment in time, and it computes:
- where the Sun and Earth sit in that point's sky, 
- how much sunlight reaches the ground and that moment and at the time range, 
- is Earth currently visible (and is communication with it possible), 
- how steep is the surface in this point.  
Then pick a second, third, fourth point and compare positions for landing, or use surface view to see how it looks from the surface!
This is important, because each lunar mission needs energy from the Sun and contact with Earth. Also it needs to land, so our program calculates steepness of the surface.
Positions come from SPICE DE440 ephemerides. Landscape data comes from LROC 100x100m squares landscape data. We calculate sun and Earth positions and use nearby terrain data to know if they are obstructed by the terrain.  
A full year of hourly samples computes in about 0.3 seconds.
details:
What it does / how it works 

Earthrise is a web app that answers the two questions every lunar mission asks of a landing site: will there be power, and can we talk to Earth? — plus can we even land here?                   

You pick a point on a 3D globe of the Moon (or type coordinates) and a moment in time. The app computes: 

  - Where the Sun and Earth sit in that point's sky — true azimuth, elevation, range and angular size.

  - How much sunlight reaches the ground — both at that instant and as an hourly time-series over any window, from one day up to a full year.

  - Whether Earth is visible — line-of-sight windows (rise, set, duration, peak elevation), so you know when a radio link is possible.

  - How steep the surface is — slope and aspect at the point, which decides whether a lander can set down safely.

Positions come from NASA SPICE DE440 ephemerides, computed in the Moon's body-fixed MOON_ME frame. Terrain comes from the LRO LROC WAC GLD100 elevation model at 100 m per pixel. Crucially, we don't assume a flat horizon: we ray-march a 360 degree horizon profile through the surrounding terrain out to 263 km, so a distant ridge actually shadows the Sun or blocks the Earth — the illumination and visibility numbers reflect real topography.

Then you drop a second, third and fourth pin and compare all four sites side by side in a ranked table, with their illumination and Earth-elevation curves overlaid on one time axis. Or switch to surface view — a first-person scene that drops you onto the real terrain, lit from the Sun's actual direction, with the Earth placed where it truly is in the sky, showing its phase.

 

Benefits & intended impact

Site selection for a lunar mission normally means stitching together separate tools for ephemerides, illumination and terrain. Earthrise collapses that into a few clicks and puts power, communication and landability on one shared time axis. A full year of hourly samples computes in about 0.3 seconds, so comparing candidate sites is interactive and fast. Every view is encoded in the URL, so a site analysis is a single shareable link — one colleague opens exactly what another was looking at. The intended impact is to make rigorous, physics-based lunar site reconnaissance accessible to mission planners, researchers, educators and students alike.

 

Tools & technologies

  - Backend: Python + FastAPI, spiceypy (the NASA SPICE toolkit) for ephemerides and frame transforms, NumPy for the terrain and insolation math, memory-mapped GLD100 DEM tiles for fast horizon ray-marching.

  - Frontend: React 18 + TypeScript + Vite, react-globe.gl for the 3D Moon, raw three.js for the first-person surface scene, ECharts (with LTTB downsampling) for the dual-axis charts, Tailwind CSS v4 + shadcn/ui, organized in a Feature-Sliced Design architecture with all state mirrored to the URL.

  - Data: SPICE DE440 kernels (NAIF/JPL), LRO LROC WAC GLD100 100 m elevation model, NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit maps for the globe texture.

  - Deployment: Dockerized backend and frontend via Docker Compose.

 

How it's creative

Most Moon tools either visualize geometry or crunch numbers; Earthrise does both and ties them together. Accounting for real terrain shadowing is what makes the illumination and comms answers trustworthy near ridges, crater rims and the poles where missions actually want to land. You can try it out yorself and view beautiful and different graphs. You will probably be the first person to see them.

The surface view turns abstract azimuth/elevation numbers into something you can intuitively see, and the four-site comparison reframes site selection as a direct, visual trade-off.

Factors we considered

- Physical accuracy: proper aberration-corrected positions, the correct body-fixed frame, slope-projected insolation, and terrain-based obstruction rather than a flat horizon.

- Speed: lazy memory-mapping of multi-gigabyte DEM tiles and efficient sampling so a year of data returns in a fraction of a second.

- Real mission constraints: power, communication and landing safety, treated as first-class outputs rather than afterthoughts.

- Usability & sharing: click-or-type input, shareable URLs, and comparison built in, so the tool fits how planning teams actually work.
